draft.title: Enzyme inhibition
card: An inhibitor is a molecule that slows down or stops an enzyme. It does this by binding to the enzyme.
A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate. It binds to the active site and blocks the substrate from entering.
A non-competitive inhibitor binds to a different part of the enzyme. This changes the shape of the active site, so the substrate no longer fits well.
In both types, the enzyme works more slowly while the inhibitor is bound. Many inhibitors can be released, so the effect may be reversed.
draft.remember: Competitive inhibitors block the active site. Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change its shape.

a.q: An inhibitor binds to a site away from the active site and changes the active site's shape. What type of inhibitor is it?
a.why: Binding away from the active site and changing its shape is non-competitive inhibition. A competitive inhibitor would sit in the active site itself.
a.clue: Where on the enzyme does the inhibitor bind?

b.q: A drug molecule closely resembles an enzyme's substrate. It enters the active site and stays there, so less substrate can bind. How does the drug act?
opts: As a competitive inhibitor, by blocking the active site
As a non-competitive inhibitor, by changing the active site
As a substrate, by speeding up the reaction
As a catalyst, by lowering the activation energy
b.why: The drug looks like the substrate and occupies the active site, so it is a competitive inhibitor. A non-competitive inhibitor would bind elsewhere, which this drug does not.
b.clue: Look at where the drug sits and what it resembles.

b.best: As a competitive inhibitor, by blocking the active site
